newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS -Russia may not need another 1997 Eurobond. [CORRECTED 17:14 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS -Russia may not need another 1997 Eurobond. [CORRECTED 17:14 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects the headline to make clear that Russia has already issued two Eurobonds this year.)
Russia said on Monday that improved tax collection meant it may be able to meet its 1997 budget targets without seeking funds on international markets.

But an analyst said he did not see how Moscow could fulfil President Boris Yeltsin's recent pledge to pay off a huge wage debt to workers and soldiers by October without running out of money by the end of the year.
Russia had planned to issue a fourth Eurobond this autumn to help fill its budget gap but Deputy Finance Minister Mikhail Kasyanov told Reuters on Monday that may not be necessary.
"By the end of the year Russia may not issue any more bonds as the situation with tax collection is improving," Kasyanov, in charge of Russia's foreign debt, told Reuters.

The state collected 100 trillion roubles ($17.3 billion), or 85 percent of taxes targeted for the first five months of 1997, compared to 69 percent in the first quarter of the year, a State Tax Service spokeswoman said. She said June collection was 25.8 trillion roubles, or 3.5 percent more than planned.
But a lot of the funds were in barter form, she said, adding she did not know how much cash had been collected.

From that cash, the state must repay 4.4 trillion roubles in wage arrears to the military and public employees by October to comply with Yeltsin's order, a Finance Ministry spokeswoman quoted Deputy Finance Minister Alexander Smirnov as saying.

"Simple mathematics shows that it is impossible for them to both pay back the arrears and to keep current with their obligations under the budget," said a Moscow brokerage analyst, who declined to be named.
"They must be accruing new debt in some form if they pay off the wage arrears out of their current revenues as their current revenues are not enough to meet their current obligations."
First Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin was quoted by Interfax new agency as saying Russia could avoid issuing a second Eurobond this year but only if revenues improved further.

The 1997 budget provides for 529.8 trillion roubles in state spending, but the government has proposed cutting expenditures by 108 trillion roubles following poor tax collection. The move has not yet been approved by parliament.

Wage arrears, rooted in low tax collection, a non-payment crisis between companies and economic stagnation, are a source of serious social discontent in Russia, leading to fairly frequent protest marches and strikes.

Yeltsin, recognising the political sensitivity of the arrears, has put priority on getting rid of them. The government managed to finish repaying 22 trillion roubles in back pensions by the July 1 deadline he set and back wages is the new target.
Ministers have squeezed big tax debtors like gas monopoly Gazprom to raise new funds and say they are continuing to press companies to pay up. But a web of debts makes this difficult.
The government is also seeking other ways to raise funds, although the Kremlin press service denied a report that Yeltsin had said Russia would ask foreign governments for help.
First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais told Yeltsin last week that it was impossible to make the October deadline.

Finance Ministry officials said revenues from Russia's previous $2.0 Eurobond, issued in June, had been used to cover the budget deficit. Russia has said it planned a new global issue this autumn and dealers estimated the volume would be between $500 million and $1 billion.
